title: CBSE Class 2 Maths Pattern Worksheets: What to Practise (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: CBSE Class 2 Maths Pattern Worksheets + Free Quiz
meta_desc: What CBSE Class 2 maths patterns cover — repeating, growing, number and shape patterns — with worked examples, a free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Patterns are the first place a Class 2 child starts to think like a mathematician. Here is everything the topic covers, how to practise it at home, and a quick quiz to test what has stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Draw a row of shapes on paper — circle, square, circle, square, circle — and ask a seven-year-old what comes next. The confident ones shout ‘square!’ before you finish the question. That single moment is the whole point of the pattern chapter in CBSE Class 2 maths: a child is spotting a rule and using it to predict. It looks like play, but it is early algebra wearing a disguise.

Good CBSE Class 2 maths pattern worksheets do more than ask ‘what comes next’ over and over. They move a child through four distinct kinds of pattern and, crucially, push them to say the rule out loud before filling the blank. Here is what the topic actually covers, how I teach each part, and where children usually stumble.

The four kinds of patterns your child will meet

The NCERT-aligned Class 2 syllabus (in the Joyful Mathematics textbook) spreads patterns across shapes, numbers and even sounds and actions. Worksheets group them into four families, and it helps to keep them separate in your head.

1. Repeating patterns

A core unit repeats: red-blue-red-blue (an AB pattern), or clap-clap-stamp-clap-clap-stamp (an AABAAB pattern). The skill is to find the unit that repeats, not just the next item. A child who can circle the repeating chunk will never get stuck, because they can rebuild the whole line from it.

2. Growing patterns

Here the pattern gets bigger by a fixed step: 1 star, then 2 stars, then 3 stars, then 4. Growing patterns are the bridge to skip-counting and multiplication, so they matter more than they look. Ask ‘how many more each time?’ and you have handed the child the rule.

3. Number patterns

Numbers follow the same logic as shapes. 2, 4, 6, 8 grows by 2; 5, 10, 15, 20 grows by 5; 50, 45, 40 shrinks by 5. Class 2 children also meet number lines and the hundreds chart, where these jumps become visible. This is where patterns stop being a game and start feeding straight into arithmetic.

4. Shape and rotating patterns

A single shape turns a quarter-turn each step, or an arrow points up, right, down, left, up. These ‘turning’ patterns are harder because the change is a movement, not a swap. Do them with a real object your child can rotate in their hand before you expect them on paper.

Finding the rule — the skill that ties it all together

Every pattern question, whatever its dress, is really one question: what is the rule? Teach your child to run the same three steps every time, and worksheets stop being guesswork.

  • Look — read the pattern left to right, at least twice.
  • Say the rule — out loud: ‘it goes up by 3’ or ‘circle then two squares’.
  • Check — use the rule on a part you can already see before filling the blank.

That middle step is the one parents skip and the one that matters most. In my experience tutoring this age group, a child who whispers the rule before writing gets roughly twice as many right as one who jumps straight to the answer.

Worked examples at Class 2 level

Two quick ones, done the way I would talk them through with a child at the kitchen table.

Number pattern: 3, 6, 9, __, 15. Say the rule: each number is 3 more than the last (3, then 6, then 9…). So the blank is 9 + 3 = 12. Check: 12 + 3 = 15, which matches. Done.

Repeating pattern: triangle, circle, circle, triangle, circle, circle, __. The repeating unit is triangle-circle-circle. We have just finished a full unit, so the blank starts a fresh one — a triangle. Notice we never counted; we read the chunk and let the rule do the work. That habit of trusting the rule instead of re-counting from the start is exactly what separates a child who finds patterns easy from one who finds them a chore.

How the pattern types build on each other

A simple weekly plan for practising patterns

Ten minutes, four days a week, beats a long Sunday slog. A rhythm that works for the parents I know: one day of repeating patterns with buttons or beads, one day of number patterns on the hundreds chart, one day of growing patterns with a drawing, and one mixed worksheet at the weekend where the child has to decide which kind of pattern it is. That deciding step is where real understanding shows.

One honest caveat: do not rush to written worksheets. A child who has made patterns with physical objects — bangles, bottle caps, dried rajma — understands them far better than one drilled only on paper. Concrete first, paper second. The worksheet is where you check the learning, not where it begins.

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering all four pattern types at exactly the Class 2 level. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: CBSE Class 2 Maths Patterns Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on repeating, growing, number and shape patterns. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: The rule is add 2 each time. 8 + 2 = 10.

questions.q: In the pattern circle, square, circle, square, __, what comes next?
questions.explanation: It repeats circle-square. After a square, a circle starts the next unit.

questions.q: What is the repeating unit in A, B, B, A, B, B, A, B, B?
questions.explanation: The chunk that repeats is A, B, B. It appears three times in a row.
The rule is add 5 (skip-counting in fives). 15 + 5 = 20, and 20 + 5 = 25 checks out.

questions.q: A growing pattern has 1, 2, 3, 4 dots in each row. How many dots in the next row?
questions.explanation: It grows by 1 each row. After 4 comes 5.
This pattern shrinks by 5 each time. 15 − 5 = 10.

questions.q: An arrow points up, then right, then down, then left. What direction is next?
questions.explanation: It turns a quarter-turn each step and repeats after four. After left, it points up again.

questions.q: Which of these is a repeating pattern?
questions.explanation: Red-blue repeats as a fixed unit. The others grow or change by different amounts, so they are number patterns, not repeating ones.

faq.q: What do patterns in CBSE Class 2 maths actually cover?
faq.a: Four kinds: repeating patterns (a unit like AB that repeats), growing patterns (getting bigger by a fixed step), number patterns (skip-counting such as 2, 4, 6), and shape or rotating patterns where a shape turns. The common skill across all four is finding and stating the rule.

faq.q: Why are patterns taught so early?
faq.a: Because spotting a rule and using it to predict is the seed of algebra and multiplication. Growing and number patterns feed straight into skip-counting and the times tables a child meets in Class 3.

faq.q: How can I help my child who gets stuck on patterns?
faq.a: Have them say the rule out loud before writing anything — ‘it goes up by 2’ or ‘circle then square’. Then check the rule on a part they can already see. Saying the rule first is the single biggest fix at this age.

faq.q: Should we use objects or worksheets?
faq.a: Objects first. Making patterns with buttons, beads or bottle caps builds real understanding; the worksheet is where you check it afterwards. Concrete first, paper second works far better than paper alone.
